body.statement:
For arbitrary real \(n\times m\) matrices \(A_1,A_0\),
\[
 \operatorname{rank}(A_1-A_0)
 \le\operatorname{rank}(A_1)+\operatorname{rank}(A_0).
\]
The converse implication from low rank of the difference to low rank of both arms fails even under the entrywise envelope \(B\): there are matrices \(A_0,A_1\) with entries bounded in absolute value by \(B\), both of rank \(n\wedge m\), whose difference has rank one.
body.proof_tex:
For every \(x\in\mathbb R^m\),
\[
 (A_1-A_0)x=A_1x-A_0x
 \in\operatorname{im}(A_1)+\operatorname{im}(A_0).
\]
Hence \(\operatorname{im}(A_1-A_0)\subseteq
\operatorname{im}(A_1)+\operatorname{im}(A_0)\).  Taking dimensions and using
\(\dim(S+T)\le\dim S+\dim T\) for finite-dimensional subspaces proves the rank inequality.

For the witness put \(s=n\wedge m\), let \((e_t)_{t=1}^n\) and \((f_t)_{t=1}^m\) be the standard bases, and define
\[
 C=\frac B2\sum_{t=1}^s e_tf_t^\top,
 \qquad A_0=C,
 \qquad A_1=C+\frac B4e_1f_1^\top.
\]
Every entry of \(A_0\) has absolute value at most \(B/2\), and every entry of \(A_1\) has absolute value at most \(3B/4\), so the declared envelope holds.  The leading \(s\times s\) diagonal block of \(A_0\) has diagonal entries \(B/2\), while that of \(A_1\) has first diagonal entry \(3B/4\) and all remaining diagonal entries \(B/2\).  Because \(B>0\), both blocks are nonsingular and both rectangular matrices have the maximal rank \(s\).  Finally,
\(A_1-A_0=(B/4)e_1f_1^\top\) has rank one.  This proves the claimed failure of the converse without making any class-containment or rate assertion.
